title: Early gameplay clip from my AI-assisted post-apocalyptic turn-based RPG — looking for feedback
author: No_Piano_1857
selftext:
I’ve been developing a small post-apocalyptic turn-based RPG and using AI tools throughout the process — not just for visuals, but also for coding support.
AI helps me with:
• solving complex gameplay logic and mechanics
• generating posters, textures and environmental concepts
• creating UI background elements and mood references
Here’s a short gameplay clip from the current early build.
I’m focusing on atmosphere, slow exploration, and tactical decision-making, but I’m still refining things like:
– combat pacing
– HUD readability
– how much info should be visible during a turn
If anyone’s into AI-assisted game development or turn-based systems, I’d really appreciate feedback on the early demo:
https://marcin4001.itch.io/arkansas-2125
Any impressions — gameplay, atmosphere, pacing, UI — are super helpful. Still very early in development.

replies.author: No_Piano_1857
replies.body:
Game Engine: Unity 6
Ai tools: ChatGpt (Posters, NPC dialogues, code for some mechanics, textures)
Gemini (textures)
When it comes to workflow, I usually sit down and fire up Unity and Visual Studio. I describe simple mechanics myself, as well as more complex features like randomization, shaders, dialogue systems, inventory, etc. But it's not like I just copy and paste without thinking. First, I read the code, try to understand it, and then I paste either the entire function or just a line. 
As for textures, I use the chat gpt generator. I enter the prompt for what I want (Usually in my native Polish, which really gives better results ). If the chos needs to be corrected, I explain it to him in the next prompt or immediately send it to Photoshop and correct, for example, badly written text. 
As for dialogue, I usually write it with gpt chat. I tell him what I want the character to say in general terms, and he describes it to me in dialogue form.

replies.author: No_Piano_1857
replies.body:
For the isometric look I’m using an orthographic camera with a fixed angle — nothing fancy.
The objects themselves are just regular 3D models; the isometric feel comes entirely from the camera setup rather than any special rendering trick.
It keeps things simple while still giving that classic iso look

comments.author: cwkx
comments.body: I wonder if the indirect lighting could be improved; right now the shadows look great in the direction they are falling, but in the other direction, there is no indirect light or occlusion, which looks flat/poor on the bottom-left of everything (e.g. https://youtu.be/b_I9fVenRIo?si=Og1vHhU50_DGGQMe&t=274 at 4:34). Given you mentioned 3D models, there could be a few ways to get cheap indirect illumination, from a single, shadow-aware ambient term from the opposite direction of your key light, tinted by nearby surfaces, light/reflection probes, or baked approaches.
